extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students interested in Oscar Wilde, Victorian literature, and literary biography
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia-style biographical overview of Oscar Wilde covering his essays, aesthetics, major works (novel and plays), trials, imprisonment, exile, and final years. Includes quotations of Wilde's aesthetic principles and descriptions of his working methods and theatrical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art is individualism
rubrics_metrics.description: "Art is individualism, and individualism is a disturbing and disintegrating force. There lies its immense value. For what it seeks is to disturb monotony of type, slavery of custom, tyranny of habit, and the reduction of man to the level of a machine."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wilde's aesthetic standard: art's value lies in its capacity to disturb social and cultural uniformity; it should challenge conventions and free individuals from mechanised conformity. Use this as a criterion when assessing the purpose/merit of artistic works — preference for works that assert individual expression and subvert habitual norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Works judged by craft, not morality
rubrics_metrics.description: Wilde's position in court: "works of art are not capable of being moral or immoral but only well or poorly made".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for evaluating art: prioritize technical quality, construction, and aesthetic success over moralistic judgments. When debating a work's merit, assess craftsmanship, vitality, and completeness rather than ethical content alone. (Context: Wilde used this defense to argue against moralistic criticism.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Societal/economic conditions for artistic flourishing (The Soul of Man Under Socialism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wilde argued that political/economic change should "convert private property into public wealth, and substituting co-operation for competition..." and that mechanisation should free human effort so it "can instead be expended on artistic creation." He also suggested the government most amenable to artists was "no government at all."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A prescriptive standard about the social conditions that enable art: assess whether material conditions (economic security, reduced necessity) and social arrangements (co-operation over competition) permit sustained artistic creation. Useful when evaluating arguments about art's social role or the environment required for artists to flourish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compose by assembling phrases, bons mots and witticisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Wilde "often composed by assembling phrases, bons mots and witticisms into a longer, cohesive work." He retained an oral tradition and wrote dialogue/essays that reflect his skills as a wit and raconteur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for prose and dialogue style: value concision, memorable aphorisms, and crafted epigrams integrated into overall structure. In assessing Wildean writing (or emulating it), look for how individual witticisms serve the work's cohesion rather than existing as isolated ornaments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface wit with subtle social subversion (comedy of society)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lady Windermere's Fan is described: "On the surface a witty comedy, there is subtle subversion underneath: 'it concludes with collusive concealment rather than collective disclosure'. The audience... are forced to soften harsh social codes in favour of a more nuanced view."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard for satirical/comedic drama: successful social comedies combine light, witty surface humor with deeper subversive critique of social mores. When evaluating such plays, examine both the comic technique and the subversive intent — effective works use wit to nudge audiences toward more nuanced moral judgments rather than explicit denunciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target audience with adroit precision (commercial and artistic balance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peter Raby: Wilde "targeted his audience with adroit precision"—he balanced an eye on Ibsen's dramatic genius and the commercial competition in London's West End.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for theatrical or literary production: measure how well a work is pitched to its intended audience and market. Successful practitioners calibrate artistic influences and commercial realities to reach the desired public without sacrificing authorial voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful construction, revision and rehearsal of plays
rubrics_metrics.description: For The Importance of Being Earnest: "Both author and producer assiduously revised, prepared and rehearsed every line, scene and setting in the months before the premiere, creating a carefully constructed representation of late-Victorian society."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Production standard: theatrical success is linked to meticulous pre‑production work — revision, staging, and rehearsal. Evaluate dramatic works on evidence of careful construction and editing; in practice, prioritize iterative refinement and collaborative rehearsal as part of making a polished production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural concision in dramatic form
rubrics_metrics.description: During rehearsal Alexander requested that Wilde shorten the play from four acts to three, which the author did.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form/structure criterion: consider economy and concision of dramatic structure — trimming acts/scenes to improve pacing and theatrical impact. When producing or assessing plays, evaluate whether the structure serves clarity and momentum; unnecessary length is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose form appropriate to intended readership (adopted proletarian ballad form)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wilde adopted the "proletarian ballad" form for The Ballad of Reading Gaol and credited the author as "C33" (his cell number), saying it would circulate among the criminal classes — "for once I will be read by my peers".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for form and audience alignment: select poetic or narrative forms that match the intended readership and rhetorical purpose. Effective work chooses genre and voice to reach and resonate with a targeted community; intentional pseudonymity or mode can shape reception and accessibility.
